balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Datadog, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

customerCohorts.title: Large-customer cohorts
customerCohorts.content:
Datadog discloses, each quarter, the number of customers whose annualized recurring revenue (ARR) is >= $100,000 and, each year, how many have crossed >= $1,000,000 ARR, plus the share of total ARR the $100K+ cohort represents.

For Datadog, Inc.: the $100K+ cohort now accounts for roughly 90% of ARR -- the bull case rests on these large accounts expanding usage (observability, security, AI) faster than the long tail of small accounts, not on adding more small logos.

What to watch:

  • $100K+ customer count growing slower than total Customers (concentration still rising)
  • % of ARR from $100K+ accounts flattening or falling -- a sign large-account expansion is stalling
  • $1M+ count is only disclosed annually, so it moves in yearly steps on this chart, not quarterly

productAdoption.title: Product adoption (platform cross-sell)
productAdoption.content:
The percentage of customers using 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10+ Datadog products out of its 30+ product portfolio (infrastructure monitoring, APM, logs, security, etc.).

For Datadog, Inc.: this is the platform/land-and-expand thesis made visible -- Net Revenue Retention is the dollar outcome of the same cross-sell motion these percentages describe. Multi-product customers spend far more per account and churn less.

What to watch:

  • The 8+ and 10+ lines are the newest, smallest cohorts -- their growth rate (not level) signals whether deep adoption is still accelerating
  • A plateau across all five lines together, not just one, would say cross-sell is stalling rather than a single product maturing
  • Compare against NetRevenueRetention: adoption climbing while retention is flat would be a disconnect worth digging into

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Datadog, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Datadog, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Datadog, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Datadog, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Datadog, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Datadog, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Datadog, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Datadog, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Datadog, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
